6º de Primaria · Inglés

Modal verbs: can, must, should

Ficha para imprimir
123456
1

Pregunta de arranquePiensa 30 segundos antes de seguir

Tres frases: «Puedo nadar», «Debes llevar casco» y «Deberías beber agua». ¿Qué diferencia hay entre «debes» y «deberías»?

Escribe o di en voz alta tu respuesta. Después .

«Debes» es una obligación (una norma): en inglés, You must wear a helmet. «Deberías» es un consejo: You should drink water. Y «puedo» es una capacidad: I can swim. Los tres son verbos modales.

2

Aprende14 apartados

Para empezar: Rules for Biscuit

Last month our family adopted a puppy. His name is Biscuit, and he is brown, fluffy and VERY naughty. On the first day, he ate my slipper, and on the second day he chewed Dad's homework folder. So we had a family meeting and wrote some rules.

Rules for Biscuit (and for us!)

  • Biscuit mustn't sleep on the sofa. He has to sleep in his basket.
  • We have to take him for a walk three times a day. My brother and I have to take turns.
  • We mustn't give him chocolate. It's dangerous for dogs.
  • Biscuit can play in the garden, but he can't go in the vegetable patch.
  • We should give him lots of love and patience.
  • Visitors don't have to be afraid. Biscuit only licks people!

Yesterday Grandma visited us. «May I give him a biscuit?» she asked. We laughed. «Yes, you can, but only a dog biscuit!»

Biscuit still isn't perfect. He might eat another slipper one day. But he is learning, and so are we.

1. What are modal verbs?

Modal verbs are special verbs that go before another verb to add a meaning: ability, permission, obligation or advice. The most common are can, must and should.

They have three golden rules: 1) the same form for all persons: «he can», not «he cans»; 2) the next verb has no to: «I can swim», not «I can to swim»; 3) no do/does in negatives and questions: «I can't», «Can you…?». En castellano: son como «poder» y «deber», pero sin conjugar.

2. Can: ability

We use can to talk about ability (capacidad, saber hacer algo): «I can ride a bike», «My sister can speak three languages», «Penguins can't fly, but they can swim very well».

For the past we use could / couldn't: «When I was five I could swim, but I couldn't read». Questions and short answers: «Can you play the guitar?» – «Yes, I can. / No, I can't». En castellano: «can» traduce «sé» o «puedo»: «I can swim» = «sé nadar».

3. Can: permission and requests

We also use can to ask for and give permission (permiso): «Can I go to the toilet, please?» – «Yes, you can». «You can't use your phone in class». And to make requests (pedir cosas): «Can you help me, please?».

A more polite way is could: «Could I open the window?», «Could you pass me the salt, please?». Consejo: en clase, pedir las cosas con Can I…, please? o Could I…? es muy educado.

4. May and might

May is a modal verb with two uses:

  • Very polite permission, especially when we speak to adults we don't know well or in formal situations: «May I come in?» «May I use your phone, please?» Answers: «Yes, of course you may.» / «I'm sorry, you may not.»
  • Possibility, like might: «It may rain later.» «She may be at home.» (puede que)

Might is used for possibility, and it shows we are even less sure: «I might go to the beach tomorrow, I don't know yet.»

From less polite to more polite, we can ask permission like this:

  • «Can I go to the toilet?» (normal, friendly)
  • «Could I go to the toilet, please?» (more polite)
  • «May I go to the toilet, please?» (very polite)

Like all modal verbs, may and might don't add -s and are followed by a verb without to: «He may know the answer.»

5. Must and mustn't: rules

We use must for obligation and strong rules: «You must wear a seat belt», «Students must be on time». We use mustn't (must not) for prohibition (prohibido): «You mustn't run in the corridor», «You mustn't feed the animals».

Careful: mustn't means «it is forbidden», not «it isn't necessary». En castellano: «you must» = «debes / tienes que»; «you mustn't» = «no debes / está prohibido».

Vídeo: Must / mustn't: school rules · PUPPI Channel (YouTube) · 363 mil visualizaciones

6. Have to and don't have to

Have to also means obligation, often rules from other people: «I have to do my homework every day», «She has to wear a uniform». It changes with the person (has to) and uses do/does: «Do you have to get up early?».

Don't have to means it is not necessary: «Tomorrow is Saturday, so I don't have to go to school». Compare: «You mustn't touch it» (prohibido) and «You don't have to come» (no hace falta). En castellano: «no tienes que» no es lo mismo que «no debes».

7. Had to: obligation in the past

Must has no past form. To talk about obligations in the past, we use had to for all persons:

  • «Yesterday I had to get up at six because we went on a trip.»
  • «My grandparents had to walk five kilometres to school.»
  • «We had to wear a uniform at my old school.»

Negative: didn't have to means it wasn't necessary: «It was Sunday, so I didn't have to go to school.» (No tuve que…)

Questions: «Did you have to study a lot for the exam?» – «Yes, I did.»

And for prohibitions in the past we use couldn't or wasn't / weren't allowed to: «When my dad was a child, he couldn't watch TV after nine o'clock.» «We weren't allowed to use mobile phones in class.»

Ask an older person: what did they have to do when they were your age? What weren't they allowed to do? You may be surprised!

Here is an example from a grandmother born in 1955: «When I was eleven, I had to help my mother every day: I had to make the beds and buy the bread. We didn't have to do much homework, but we had to learn lots of things by heart. Girls weren't allowed to wear trousers at my school, and we couldn't talk in the corridors.» How different is your life?

Vídeo: Modal Verbs: Have to and Must: The Grammar Gameshow Episode 5 · BBC Learning English (YouTube) · 290 mil visualizaciones

8. Should: advice

We use should to give advice (consejos) and say what is a good idea: «You should go to bed early», «You look tired. You should rest». Shouldn't says it's a bad idea: «You shouldn't eat so many sweets».

To ask for advice: «What should I do?», «Should I tell the teacher?». En castellano: «should» es «deberías». Es más suave que must: no es una norma, es una recomendación.

9. More ways to give advice

Should is the most common way to give advice, but there are other friendly and polite ways to help a friend:

  • You'd better (= you had better) + verb: strong advice, often a warning. «You'd better take an umbrella. It's going to rain.» Negative: «You'd better not be late.»
  • Why don't you…? a friendly suggestion: «Why don't you ask the teacher?»
  • If I were you, I'd…: imagine you are the other person. «If I were you, I'd say sorry.»
  • How about / What about + -ing?: «How about studying together?»
  • Ought to: similar to should, a bit more formal. «You ought to drink more water.»

And when you need advice, you can ask: «What should I do?» «Do you think I should…?» «What would you do?»

Good advice is kind and respectful. Listen first, then give your advice, and remember the other person decides in the end.

10. Choosing the right modal

Ask yourself: is it an ability? → can. Is it permission? → can / could. Is it a rule or obligation? → must / have to. Is it forbidden? → mustn't. Is it advice? → should.

Examples: «You must stop at a red light» (rule). «You should wear a coat, it's cold» (advice). «I can touch my toes» (ability). «You mustn't use the lift in a fire» (forbidden).

11. Reading: rules at the swimming pool

Read the poster: «SWIMMING POOL RULES. You must have a shower before you swim. You must wear a swimming cap. You mustn't run around the pool. You mustn't eat in the water. Children under eight must be with an adult. You can use the slide from 11 to 1. Advice: you should wear flip-flops and you should drink water after swimming.»

Find two obligations, two prohibitions, one permission and one piece of advice.

12. Let's practise: class rules and advice

In groups, write the rules for your classroom: «We must listen when someone is speaking», «We mustn't shout», «We can read a book when we finish». Make a poster.

Then play «Problem and advice»: one student says a problem and the others give advice. «I can't sleep.» – «You should read a book», «You shouldn't use your tablet at night». Consejo: recuerda la regla de oro: después de un modal, el verbo va sin to y sin -s.

13. Signs and notices

When you travel to an English-speaking country, you will see lots of signs and notices. Many of them express obligation, prohibition or advice, but in a very short way, without modal verbs:

  • Prohibition (you mustn't): «No entry», «No smoking», «Do not touch», «Keep off the grass», «No parking», «Do not feed the animals».
  • Obligation (you must / you have to): «Keep left», «Please queue here», «Seat belts must be worn», «Dogs must be kept on a lead».
  • Warning (be careful): «Caution: wet floor», «Danger: high voltage», «Mind the gap» (on the London Underground: be careful with the space between the train and the platform).
  • Information: «Exit», «Toilets», «Push / Pull», «Open 9–5», «Out of order» (it doesn't work).

To explain a sign, we can use modal verbs: «Keep off the grass» means «You mustn't walk on the grass». «Please queue here» means «You have to wait in a line here».

Signs often use pictures too, so people who don't speak the language can understand them. A red circle with a line usually means «No», a red triangle means «Warning» and a blue circle usually means something you must do.

Vídeo: Signs and Symbols | Traffic Signs · Teacher Lis TV (YouTube) · 666 mil visualizaciones

14. Rules around the world

Every country has its own rules and customs. Here are some that may surprise you:

  • In the United Kingdom, Ireland, Japan and Australia, you have to drive on the left.
  • In Singapore, shops can't sell normal chewing gum. The government banned it in 1992 to keep the streets clean.
  • In Japan, you have to take off your shoes when you enter a house, and also in some schools and temples. You shouldn't blow your nose at the table or talk loudly on the phone on trains.
  • In the United States, in most places, you should leave a tip in restaurants: it's part of the waiter's pay.
  • In many countries in Europe, including Spain, children have to use a special car seat until they are tall enough.
  • In Venice, Italy, tourists mustn't feed the pigeons in St Mark's Square.

When you travel, it's a good idea to learn the local rules before you arrive. As people say, «When in Rome, do as the Romans do»: when you are in a new place, you should follow its customs.

Ejemplos resueltos

Ejemplo 1. Complete: «Dogs ___ climb trees.» (ability, negative)

  1. Capacidad → can.
  2. Negativa → can't.

Resultado: Dogs can't climb trees.

Ejemplo 2. Give advice: «I'm hungry.»

  1. Consejo → should + verbo.
  2. Sin to.

Resultado: You should eat a sandwich.

Ejemplo 3. Choose: «You (mustn't / don't have to) cross the road when the light is red.»

  1. Es una prohibición, no algo opcional.

Resultado: You mustn't cross the road when the light is red.

Ejemplo 4. Make it more polite: «Can I open the window?»

  1. Could I…, please? is more polite.
  2. May I…, please? is very polite.

Resultado: May I open the window, please?

Ejemplo 5. Past: «I have to wear a uniform.» (last year)

  1. Must and have to change to had to.
  2. Same for all persons.

Resultado: Last year I had to wear a uniform.

Errores típicos

  • Poner to tras el modal: «I can to swim» → «I can swim».
  • Poner -s: «she cans», «he musts» → «she can», «he must».
  • Usar do con modales: «Do you can…?» → «Can you…?».
  • Confundir mustn't (prohibido) con don't have to (no hace falta).
  • Usar must para un simple consejo: «You must try this cake» (mejor «You should try»).
  • Decir «I musted» o «I must yesterday»: en pasado se usa had to.
  • Escribir «He mays» o «may to»: los modales no llevan -s ni to.

PracticaResponde sin mirar arriba. Equivocarse aquí también enseña.

Ejercicios (24)

Hazlos en tu cuaderno y después abre la solución.

Nivel básico

  1. Write two things you can do and one you can't.

    Ver solución
    Model answer: I can swim. I can draw. I can't play the piano.

  2. Make a question: «You can speak French.»

    Ver solución
    Can you speak French?

  3. Past: «I can read.» (when I was six)

    Ver solución
    I could read when I was six.

  4. Make it very polite: «Can I use your pencil?»

    Ver solución
    May I use your pencil, please?

  5. Complete in the past: «Yesterday I ___ (have to) clean my room.»

    Ver solución
    had to.

  6. What does «Out of order» mean?

    Ver solución
    It doesn't work.

  7. Complete: «You'd ___ take a coat. It's cold.»

    Ver solución
    better.

  8. In which country can't shops sell normal chewing gum?

    Ver solución
    In Singapore.

Nivel medio

  1. Ask for permission to go out.

    Ver solución
    Can I go out, please? / Could I go out, please?

  2. Complete: «You ___ smoke in hospitals.»

    Ver solución
    mustn't.

  3. Complete: «It's Sunday. I ___ get up early.» (no hace falta)

    Ver solución
    don't have to.

  4. Give advice: «I've got a headache.»

    Ver solución
    You should rest / You should take a break.

  5. Correct: «She musts do her homework.»

    Ver solución
    She must do her homework.

  6. Write the negative: «I had to go to school on Saturday.»

    Ver solución
    I didn't have to go to school on Saturday.

  7. Explain the sign «Keep off the grass» with a modal verb.

    Ver solución
    You mustn't walk on the grass.

  8. Give advice with «Why don't you…?»: your friend is bored.

    Ver solución
    Why don't you read a book / play outside?

  9. Write a sentence with «may» for possibility.

    Ver solución
    Open answer. Example: It may rain this afternoon.

  10. What must Biscuit not do?

    Ver solución
    He mustn't sleep on the sofa (or eat chocolate).

Nivel avanzado

  1. Translate: «No deberías ver tanta tele.»

    Ver solución
    You shouldn't watch so much TV.

  2. Write three rules for a library.

    Ver solución
    Model answer: You must be quiet. You mustn't eat. You can borrow three books.

  3. Interview an older person: write three things they had to do and two things they weren't allowed to do.

    Ver solución
    Open answer.

  4. Your friend wants to stay up all night playing video games before an exam. Give advice in three different ways.

    Ver solución
    Open answer.

  5. Design three signs for your school and explain each one with a modal verb.

    Ver solución
    Open answer.

  6. Explain the saying «When in Rome, do as the Romans do».

    Ver solución
    When you are in a new place, you should follow its customs.

Explícalo con tus palabrasComo si se lo contaras a alguien de un curso menor

¿Has nombrado estas ideas?
★

Situación de aprendizajeA guide for visitors

La clase prepara una guía en inglés con normas y consejos para alumnos de intercambio que visitarán el colegio y la localidad.

Pasos

  1. Haced una lista de normas del colegio con must, mustn't, have to y don't have to.
  2. Diseñad carteles en inglés para lugares del colegio (biblioteca, comedor, patio).
  3. Escribid consejos para visitar vuestra localidad con should, you'd better y why don't you.
  4. Montad la guía y presentadla con un juego de rol de alumno nuevo y anfitrión.

Producto final: Una guía bilingüe de normas y consejos con carteles para el colegio.

Cómo se valora

  • Uses modal verbs correctly.
  • Talks about past obligations with had to.
  • Gives advice in different ways.
  • Writes clear signs and notices.

Tarjetas de repasoToca la tarjeta para darle la vuelta

Según cómo respondas, la tarjeta vuelve mañana, en 3, en 7 o en 21 días.

Para familias

  • Escribid en inglés tres normas de casa con must / mustn't y pegadlas en la nevera.
  • Jugad a «problema y consejo»: uno cuenta un problema y el otro responde con should.
  • Repasad juntos las tarjetas del paso 6 dos minutos al día durante una semana.

Para profesores

Saberes: Expresión de capacidad, permiso, obligación, prohibición y consejo; verbos modales (Lengua Extranjera) (RD 157/2022, tercer ciclo de Primaria).

  • Cartel de normas de clase en inglés.
  • Juego «problema y consejo» por parejas.
  • Encuesta de habilidades «Can you…?» con gráfico.

Revisado el 22 de noviembre de 2026.

Qué vas a aprender

  • Use can and can't for ability, permission and possibility
  • Use must and mustn't for rules and obligation
  • Use should and shouldn't to give advice (consejos)
  • Remember the grammar of modal verbs: no -s, no to, no do
  • Use may and might for possibility and polite permission
  • Talk about past obligations with had to
  • Give advice in different ways
  • Understand signs, notices and rules in other countries

Palabras clave

modal verbs · can / can't · could · must / mustn't · have to · should / shouldn't · ability · permission · obligation · advice

Tiempo

80 minutos hoy + 2 minutos en cada repaso
